title: Do we need an AI policy before we use this?
text: Someone on a legal team asks if they need an AI policy before rolling out a new tool. Wrong first word. What they actually need is an inventory. Lay 'em, take them through it. You could write a

title: A policy only covers what's named
text: Policy tomorrow, a rule about which AI tools are allowed, but a policy can only govern the tools someone remembered to name in it. The ones adopted quietly slip past every time because the policy never knew they existed. What actually closes that gap isn't a rule about what's allowed, it's a live list of what's actually running. Four things go

title: Four fields — the anchor
text: In for every tool on that list. What it does, what data touches it, who owns it, and a risk tier set by how sensitive that data is. Watch the Anchor, the contract review tool your litigation team quietly started using last spring. Nobody wrote it into any policy because nobody wrote it down anywhere. That tool goes through the same four

title: Logged, not cleared
text: Fields as everything else logged, tiered by risk, given an owner, and now it's visible instead of running unnoticed. But an entry doesn't mean the tool is safe. The risk tier is a flag for review, not a green light. And a finished-looking list doesn't mean nothing's missing, either. The next tool adopted tomorrow needs the same four fields before the list can call itself current. You can't govern an AI tool you

title: Carry-out
text: Haven't listed. Build the inventory before you write the policy. The policy only works once you know what it has to cover.

title: Your turn
text: Your turn. Here's the prompt. Read it with me. List every AI tool your team used this month. Drafting help, research, search, document review, anything. For each one, write down what it does, what data goes through it, and who owns it. If any row is missing an owner, that's the gap the inventory just found. Lay 'em in for Bear. What's an AI inventory? Lay 'em in for Bear.
